wv_bubba_city.blurb: Bubba City is a sector on the north and east side of the New River Gorge, near Fayetteville, West Virginia. About fifteen separate crags are scattered through it, and most cliffs get morning shade and afternoon sun. Sport climbing is the main attraction, with trad filling in, and the grades are weighted toward 5.10 through 5.12 with a healthy supply of 5.7 to 5.9 and a few 5.13s. Sandstonia, Ames Wall, Head Wall and Beer Wall are the biggest walls, and Head Wall is praised as having the best rock here, in white and orange stone.

ca_susanville_area.blurb: Susanville is a small town where the Sierra Nevada gives way to the Cascades, and within about twenty minutes the scenery shifts from alpine woodland to juniper and sagebrush ridgelines, black oak forest and high desert. The crags use granite, basalt, monzonite and rhyolite. Trad is by far the largest share, with some sport and a bouldering cluster in Lone Valley, and most grades fall in the 5.9 to 5.12 range, 5.10 being the busiest. Pigeon Cliff is the main draw, a compact roadside wall of columnar basalt with splitter cracks and steep lines about 90 feet tall. Sunny winter days suit it best, and summer mornings stay shaded in the amphitheater. Tom's Thumb, Lone Rock and Cold Stream round out the area.

co_thunder_ridge.blurb: Thunder Ridge is a long granite outcrop in the South Platte, about two hours from Boulder and an hour from Colorado Springs, so crowds stay thin. Its roughly 200 routes are spread across many separate crags, such as Brown Wall, The Quarry, Valhalla and Wasp Canyon. The rock is steep, highly featured granite with a pebbly texture, giving vertical to slightly overhanging faces with incut edges. Trad leads, sport is a solid second, and the grades center on 5.10 and 5.11, with a good number of 5.12s and a small supply of 5.7 to 5.9. Most walls face south and stay warm, so winter days work well, while a few canyons hold shade for summer.

nh_whitehorse_ledge.blurb: Whitehorse Ledge is a granite cliff in North Conway, less than a mile from its neighbor Cathedral Ledge, and it is far slabbier, especially on the right-hand side. There the Slabs offer long friction climbing at low angles, often with sparse protection, and routes reach around 800 feet and many pitches. The South Buttress is steeper, with face climbing on bolted and gear-protected lines. Trad dominates, with a little sport and a good number of boulder problems. Grades run from 5.4 to 5.12, with the greatest concentration from 5.9 to 5.11, though much of the slab climbing is far easier. Many shorter one and two pitch climbs sit near the base, and the summit slabs are sunny.

wa_upper_town_wall.blurb: The Upper Town Wall is the big cliff looming above Index, in the Skykomish Valley about an hour east of Seattle. Routes are both short and long, free and aided, with sport and trad nearly even and a handful of aid lines. Grades skew hard, with most routes between 5.10 and 5.12 and a notable group at 5.13 and 5.14, and the grading has a reputation for feeling stiff. Climbing mixes sustained cracks, steep gear-protected faces and quartz edges high up. The Central Wall Area is the largest section, while the Cheeks tend to stay dry in the rain and are easy to rig for top ropes. May through September is the best stretch.

yt_whitehorse.blurb: Whitehorse climbing is a collection of short crags close to town, on granite, limestone and basalt, with very short approaches. Sport is the main style, with trad, top-rope, a set of boulder problems and a little mixed. Grades center on 5.8 to 5.10, with fewer harder lines and a spread of easier ones. Rock Gardens is granite of great quality, with mostly 10 metre routes in a mix of sun and shade, and it is the easiest to get to. Grey Mountain holds limestone chunks on its southwest face, mainly sport. Other sub-areas include Eagle's Nest, McIntyre Creek and Vinyl Village. Golden Canyon offers granite crack climbing.
